<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par150 />''where then is...?'' However, {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹא}} may also be placed at the end of the entire question ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=1}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=10}}, since either {{GHGheb|text=אֱהִי}} is a dialectical form of {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה}}, or {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה}} should be read instead of it) or at the beginning of the question proper, after a strongly emphasized word, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=37}}.<ref>On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=24}} and 24:25 {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹ}} is not prefixed to the {{GHGheb|text=מִי}}, but appended to the conditional sentence.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|m}}
(''e'') Sometimes one interrogative governs two co-ordinate clauses, the first of which should rather be subordinated to the second, so that the interrogative word strictly speaking affects only the second; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=4}} after {{GHGheb|text=מַדּוּעַ|translate=wherefore looked I... and it brought forth?}} i.e. wherefore brought it forth, while I looked, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=2}}; after {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=4}}, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=22}} (read {{GHGheb|text=הַאִישׁ}}); after {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=20}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=4}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־מִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=25}}.<ref>Cf. the analogous sentences after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן|translate=because}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=35|verse=17}}; after causal {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=23}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=1}}; likewise after {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} § 153 at the end; after {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=12}}–14, 25:3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=28}}.</ref> But {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=2}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} 4:21 are separated from the verb to which they belong by the insertion of a conditional clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|n}}
'''3.''' The affirmative answer is generally expressed, as in Latin, by repeating the emphatic word in the question (or with the second person changed to the first, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=58}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=11}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=32|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=17}}. (On {{GHGheb|text=וָיֵשׁ|translate=if it be so}} in the corrected text of {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=15}}, see § 159 dd.) As a negative answer the simple {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is sometimes sufficient, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=22}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|152|c}}; and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}} the simple {{GHGheb|text=אָֽיִן}} equivalent to ''no'' or ''no one''.<section end=par150 />

<section begin=par151 />{{GHGpar-heading|151|Desiderative Sentences}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|a}}
A wish may be expressed not only by the simple imperfect ({{GHGpar|107|n}}), cohortative (§ 108, especially with {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} {{GHGpar|108|c}}), jussive (§ 109; with {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} {{GHGpar|109|b}}), imperative ({{GHGpar|110|a}}), perfect consecutive ({{GHGpar|112|aa}}) or by a simple noun-clause ({{GHGpar|116|r}}, note, and {{GHGpar|141|g}}) but also in the following ways:—

'''1.''' By exclamations in the form of ''interrogative'' clauses:<ref>The transition from a question to a wish may be seen, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=4}} ''who shall give us flesh to eat?'' i.e. ''O that we had flesh to eat!''</ref> especially sentences with {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} followed by the imperfect as being the mood of that which is still unfulfilled but possible, and hence also of that which is desired, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יְשִׂמֵ֫נִי שֹׁפֵט|translate=who maketh me judge?}} i.e. ''O that I were made judge!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=15}}. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} with the perfect ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=1}}, &c.) or participle ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=22}}, &c.), rather expresses a rhetorical question, i.e. a denial, cf. {{GHGpar|150|d}}. Especially frequent is the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} (prop. ''who gives?'') to introduce all kinds of desiderative clauses (see under b).—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=10}} the desiderative clause proper is co-ordinated with an interrogative clause,<section end=par151 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
